title: Twin Mounds Site
summary: In Ballard County, Twin Mounds was a Mississippian center with two platform mounds around a plaza, occupied from about 1200 to 1450 CE.
bodyMarkdown:
The Twin Mounds site, also called the Nolan site, is a Mississippian mound center in Ballard County. It was a regional center for about two and a half centuries. One rare carved pipe from the site has drawn attention far beyond Kentucky.

## The site

An account of [the Twin Mounds site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin_Mounds_Site) records it as two site numbers, 15BA2 and 15BA14. It describes a regional administrative center with two large platform mounds around a central plaza. In the village area, designated 15BA14, the midden is as much as 2 meters thick.

Platform mounds like these were a hallmark of the [Mississippian culture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Mississippian_culture), which spread across the Midwest, Southeast and Mid-South from about AD 800 to 1600. Its communities built large earthen platforms to hold the homes of leaders and ceremonial buildings.

## When people lived there

The main occupation dates from 1200 to about 1450 CE, during the Dorena and Medley phases of the local chronology. Some pottery from the earlier Late Woodland period was also found.

## The effigy pipe

Excavations at Twin Mounds found a rare human effigy pipe in the style of Cahokia, the great Mississippian center in Illinois. It is carved from Missouri flint clay, a soft red pipestone found only in eastern Missouri. The pipe stands 17.8 centimeters (7 inches) tall.

The pipe shows a crouching nude man leaning slightly forward on a small pedestal. It closely resembles the "Chunkey player" figurine from the Hughes site in Oklahoma. Many male flint-clay figures from Cahokia have been linked to the Red Horn stories of Siouan oral tradition, but it is unclear which episode, if any, this one shows. In 2004 the pipe, then in a private collection, was lent to the Art Institute of Chicago for the exhibition "Hero, Hawk, and Open Hand: American Indian Art of the Ancient Midwest and South."

## Kentucky today

Because Twin Mounds is a protected site, its location is shared here only at the county level. Other Mississippian centers in Kentucky include the [Tolu site](/stories/tolu-site-mississippian-mounds-on-the-lower-ohio/) and the Jonathan site. The mounds were built and used by Native communities over many generations and deserve respect.
